claim: Images taken by transmission electron microscopes are usually affected by lens aberrations and image defocus.
source: Images taken by transmission electron microscopes are usually affected by lens aberrations and image defocus, among other factors.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general property of TEM imaging.

claim: Distortions from lens aberrations and defocus can be modeled in reciprocal space using the contrast transfer function (CTF).
source: These distortions can be modeled in reciprocal space using the contrast transfer function (CTF).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established method in the field.

claim: Accurate estimation and correction of the CTF is essential for restoring the high-resolution signal in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM).
source: Accurate estimation and correction of the CTF is essential for restoring the high-resolution signal in cryogenic electron microscopy (cryoEM).
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental requirement in cryoEM.

claim: Algorithms for CTF estimation were previously described in the cisTEM software package.
source: Previously, we described the implementation of algorithms for this task in the cisTEM software package (Grant et al., 2018).
evidence: This references prior work by the authors with a citation.

claim: Taking sample characteristics such as thickness and tilt into account can improve CTF estimation.
source: Here we show that taking sample characteristics, such as thickness and tilt, into account can improve CTF estimation.
evidence: This is a primary claim of the manuscript supported by the data presented.

claim: Measurement of sample thickness and geometry is particularly important when imaging cellular samples.
source: This is particularly important when imaging cellular samples, where measurement of sample thickness and geometry derived from accurate modeling of the Thon ring pattern helps judging the quality of the sample.
evidence: This is stated as a specific application and importance of the method.

claim: The improved CTF estimation has been implemented in CTFFIND5.
source: This improved CTF estimation has been implemented in CTFFIND5, a new version of the cisTEM program CTFFIND.
evidence: This describes the software implementation of the method.

claim: The accuracy of CTF estimates was evaluated using images of tilted aquaporin crystals and eukaryotic cells thinned by focused ion beam milling.
source: We evaluated the accuracy of these estimates using images of tilted aquaporin crystals and eukaryotic cells thinned by focused ion beam milling.
evidence: This describes the validation approach used in the study.

claim: CTFFIND5 can measure sample tilt with an accuracy of 3° with micrographs of sufficient quality.
source: We estimate that with micrographs of sufficient quality CTFFIND5 can measure sample tilt with an accuracy of 3° and sample thickness with an accuracy of 5 nm.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation studies.

claim: CTFFIND5 can measure sample thickness with an accuracy of 5 nm with micrographs of sufficient quality.
source: We estimate that with micrographs of sufficient quality CTFFIND5 can measure sample tilt with an accuracy of 3° and sample thickness with an accuracy of 5 nm.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the validation studies.

claim: CryoEM has become a widely used method to image biomolecules at high resolution, both in solution and within the cell.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of biological specimens at cryogenic temperatures (cryoEM) has become a widely used method to image biomolecules at high resolution, both in solution and within the cell.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: CryoEM images have to be corrected for the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the microscope to retrieve the high-resolution signal.
source: To retrieve the high-resolution signal, the cryoEM images have to be corrected for the contrast transfer function (CTF) of the microscope.
evidence: This describes a necessary processing step in cryoEM.

claim: Common parameters used to describe the CTF include astigmatic defocus, spherical aberration of the objective lens, and phase shift introduced by a phase plate.
source: Common parameters used to describe the CTF include an astigmatic defocus, the spherical aberration of the objective lens, and if appropriate, a phase shift introduced by a phase plate.
evidence: This lists standard CTF parameters used in the field.

claim: Defocus and phase shift parameters are commonly estimated by fitting the Thon ring pattern in the power spectrum of micrographs to a modeled power spectrum.
source: The defocus and phase shift parameters are commonly estimated by fitting the Thon ring pattern (Thon, 1971) in the power spectrum of micrographs to a modeled power spectrum.
evidence: This describes the standard method for CTF parameter estimation with a citation.

claim: The program CTFFIND4 has been developed for CTF parameter estimation.
source: The program CTFFIND4 (Rohou and Grigorieff, 2015) has been developed for this task and the model and conventions to describe the CTF are widely adopted in the field.
evidence: This references prior software development with a citation.

claim: The CTF model and conventions used in CTFFIND4 are widely adopted in the field.
source: The program CTFFIND4 (Rohou and Grigorieff, 2015) has been developed for this task and the model and conventions to describe the CTF are widely adopted in the field.
evidence: This is a statement about the acceptance of CTFFIND4 in the field.

claim: CTFFIND4 considers the whole imaged sample to be at the same objective defocus.
source: A limitation of CTFFIND4 is that it considers the whole imaged sample to be at the same objective defocus, which is a reasonable assumption for flat and thin samples, as is common in single-particle cryoEM.
evidence: This describes a specific limitation of the previous software version.

claim: The assumption of uniform defocus is reasonable for flat and thin samples common in single-particle cryoEM.
source: A limitation of CTFFIND4 is that it considers the whole imaged sample to be at the same objective defocus, which is a reasonable assumption for flat and thin samples, as is common in single-particle cryoEM.
evidence: This justifies when the CTFFIND4 assumption is valid.

claim: The increased thickness of cryoEM samples of cells may introduce additional modulations in the Thon ring pattern.
source: However, the increased thickness of cryoEM samples of cells may introduce additional modulations in the Thon ring pattern (Tichelaar et al., 2020) that can lead to errors in the CTF modeling when not accounted for.
evidence: This describes a problem with thick samples, supported by a citation.

claim: Additional modulations in the Thon ring pattern from thick samples can lead to errors in CTF modeling when not accounted for.
source: However, the increased thickness of cryoEM samples of cells may introduce additional modulations in the Thon ring pattern (Tichelaar et al., 2020) that can lead to errors in the CTF modeling when not accounted for.
evidence: This describes the consequence of not accounting for sample thickness.

claim: Samples of cells are often tilted with respect to the optical axis of the microscope.
source: Furthermore, samples of cells are often tilted with respect to the optical axis of the microscope, either unintentionally due to thinning methods such as cryogenic focused ion beam (FIB) milling, or intentionally during electron cryo-tomography imaging.
evidence: This describes a common characteristic of cellular cryoEM samples.

claim: Sample tilt can occur unintentionally due to thinning methods such as cryogenic focused ion beam (FIB) milling.
source: Furthermore, samples of cells are often tilted with respect to the optical axis of the microscope, either unintentionally due to thinning methods such as cryogenic focused ion beam (FIB) milling, or intentionally during electron cryo-tomography imaging.
evidence: This describes one source of sample tilt.

claim: Sample tilt can occur intentionally during electron cryo-tomography imaging.
source: Furthermore, samples of cells are often tilted with respect to the optical axis of the microscope, either unintentionally due to thinning methods such as cryogenic focused ion beam (FIB) milling, or intentionally during electron cryo-tomography imaging.
evidence: This describes another source of sample tilt.

claim: The effects of sample tilt and thickness are strongest at high resolution, where the Thon rings are more tightly spaced.
source: In both cases the effects are strongest at high resolution, where the Thon rings are more tightly spaced.
evidence: This describes where the effects are most pronounced.

claim: CTFFIND5 can fit the modulations of the Thon ring patterns and determine sample thickness and tilt using an extended CTF model with additional parameters.
source: Here, we describe new features of CTFFIND5 that can fit the modulations of the Thon ring patterns and determine sample thickness and tilt using an extended CTF model with additional parameters.
evidence: This describes the main capabilities of the new software.

claim: CTFFIND5 increases the fidelity of the fit, as Thon rings at higher resolution can now be fitted reliably.
source: This not only increases the fidelity of the fit, as Thon rings at higher resolution can now be fitted reliably, but also gives valuable insight into the geometry of the sample that can aid the experimentalist.
evidence: This describes a benefit of the new method.

claim: CTFFIND5 gives valuable insight into the geometry of the sample that can aid the experimentalist.
source: This not only increases the fidelity of the fit, as Thon rings at higher resolution can now be fitted reliably, but also gives valuable insight into the geometry of the sample that can aid the experimentalist.
evidence: This describes another benefit of the new method.

claim: Tilt estimation in CTFFIND5 follows a strategy similar to the implementation in CTFTILT.
source: Tilt estimation in CTFFIND5 follows a strategy that is similar to the implementation in CTFTILT (Mindell and Grigorieff, 2003).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach with a citation to prior work.

claim: It is assumed that the defocus variation across the sample can be described by a tilted plane.
source: It is assumed that the defocus variation across the sample can be described by a tilted plane.
evidence: This describes a key assumption of the tilt model.

claim: Fits are evaluated using correlation coefficients between modeled CTFs and Thon ring patterns.
source: Fits are evaluated using correlation coefficients between modeled CTFs and Thon ring patterns.
evidence: This describes the scoring method for the fits.

claim: Tilt correction results in the observation of Thon rings at higher spatial resolution.
source: As expected, the correction results in the observation of Thon rings at higher spatial resolution (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a result demonstrated in Figure 1c.

claim: Correcting for an estimated moderate tilt of 12.3° improved the highest resolution at which a reasonable fit could be obtained from 5.9 Å to 4.6 Å in a representative micrograph.
source: In this example, correcting for the estimated moderate tilt of 12.3° improved the highest resolution at which a reasonable fit could be obtained from 5.9 Å to 4.6 Å.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative result from a representative example.

claim: The power spectrum appears less noisy after tilt correction, which can be attributed to some low-pass filtering that occurs with the interpolation of the Thon ring patterns of individual tiles.
source: The power spectrum also appears less noisy, which can be attributed to some low-pass filtering that occurs with the interpolation of the Thon ring patterns of individual tiles to perform the tilt correction.
evidence: This explains an observed effect of the tilt correction procedure.

claim: The results of CTFFIND5 agree well with aquaporin crystal tilt information from crystallographic analysis.
source: Overall, the results of CTFFIND5 agree well with the aquaporin crystals information.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results using aquaporin crystals.

claim: The average discrepancy between CTFFIND5 and crystallographic analysis was 1.9° for the tilt axis direction and 1.5° for the tilt angle in aquaporin crystal images.
source: The average discrepancy was 1.9° for the tilt axis direction and 1.5° for the tilt angle.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the aquaporin crystal validation.

claim: The estimated tilt angle shows a roughly linear relationship with the nominal stage tilt in tilt series data.
source: The estimated tilt angle shows a roughly linear relationship with the nominal stage tilt, but since CTFFIND5 reports only positive tilt angles the overall plot has a V-shape.
evidence: This describes the relationship observed in tilt series analysis.

claim: In both tilt series examples there is an offset of about 20° between nominal and estimated tilts, which is due to the pre-tilt of the specimen caused by FIB milling at a shallow angle.
source: Notably, in both examples there is an offset of about 20° between nominal and estimated tilts, which is due to the pre-tilt of the specimen caused by FIB milling at a shallow angle.
evidence: This explains an observed systematic offset in the tilt series data.

claim: The estimated tilt axis angles of 178.2° and 179.8° are consistent with the SerialEM calibration of 178.4° and 176.3° for the stage tilt axis.
source: The fitting resulted in an estimated tilt axis angle of 178.2° and 179.8°, respectively, which is consistent with the SerialEM calibration of 178.4° and 176.3° for the stage tilt axis.
evidence: This compares CTFFIND5 estimates with independent calibration values.

claim: The estimated pre-tilt values of 20.6° and –21.9° are consistent with a FIB-milling angle of 20° and opposite orientation of the grids relative to the milling direction.
source: The estimated pre-tilt values were 20.6 °and –21.9°, consistent with a FIB-milling angle of 20° and opposite orientation of the grids relative to the milling direction.
evidence: This validates the pre-tilt estimates against known experimental parameters.

claim: The pre-tilt axis angles of 171.8° and 183.8° are consistent with the error expected from manually aligning the milling direction when inserting grids into the microscope.
source: The pre-tilt axis angles were estimated as 171.8° and 183.8°, which is consistent with the error expected from manually aligning the milling direction when inserting grids into the microscope.
evidence: This explains the observed variation in pre-tilt axis angles.

claim: For the first tilt series, accuracy estimates were 2.08° and 2.58° for tilt and axis angles, respectively.
source: For the first tilt series we obtained accuracy estimates of 2.08° and 2.58° for tilt and axis angles, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative accuracy measurement from tilt series validation.

claim: In the second tilt series the accuracy estimates were 3.95° and 9.47° for tilt and axis angles, respectively.
source: In the second tilt series the accuracy estimates were 3.95° and 9.47°.
evidence: This is a quantitative accuracy measurement from tilt series validation.

claim: The accuracy of tilt estimation in tilt series was lower than for tilted aquaporin crystals, presumably due to the relatively short exposure of each micrograph in the tilt series.
source: In both cases the accuracy was lower than for the tilted aquaporin crystals, presumably due to the relatively short exposure of each micrograph in the tilt series.
evidence: This compares accuracy across different datasets and provides an explanation.

claim: The substantially higher mean differences in the second tilt series suggest that the accuracy is highly dependent on the quality of the underlying data.
source: However, the substantially higher mean differences in the second tilt series suggest that the accuracy is highly dependent on the quality of the underlying data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the two tilt series results.

claim: For FIB-milled samples, Thon ring-like modulation can be observed in the power spectrum at higher resolution than suggested by the goodness-of-fit estimate, even after correcting for sample tilt.
source: Even after correcting for sample tilt we found that for FIB-milled samples we often could observe Thon ring-like modulation in the power spectrum at higher resolution than suggested by the goodness-of-fit estimate (Figure 3b, top plot).
evidence: This is an observation from FIB-milled samples shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The modulations observed at higher resolution in FIB-milled samples are out of phase with the predicted modulations, as described by McMullan et al., 2015, and Tichelaar et al., 2020.
source: These modulations are out of phase with the predicted modulations, as described by McMullan et al., 2015, and Tichelaar et al., 2020.
evidence: This describes the nature of the observed modulations with citations to prior work.

claim: An extension of the CTF model as described by McMullan et al., 2015 was implemented in CTFFIND5.
source: We therefore implemented an extension of the CTF model as described by McMullan et al., 2015; Figure 3a.
evidence: This describes the implementation of a model from the literature.

claim: For some images, the thickness could be well estimated by assuming that the goodness-of-fit resolution estimate obtained using the old model corresponds to the first node in the modulation function.
source: For some images we found that the thickness could be well estimated by assuming that the goodness-of-fit resolution estimate obtained using the old model implemented in CTFFIND4 corresponds to the first node in the modulation function, according to Equation 7.
evidence: This describes a method for initial thickness estimation.

claim: With the new model in CTFFIND5, estimated CTF parameters were very similar to those from CTFFIND4, but the fit extended to higher resolution.
source: With our new model, estimated CTF parameters were very similar to those from CTFFIND4, but the fit in CTFFIND5 extended to higher resolution (Figure 3b).
evidence: This compares results between CTFFIND4 and CTFFIND5, shown in Figure 3b.

claim: In images with defocus values under 1 µm and sample thickness over 200 nm, CTFFIND4 could fit the power spectrum before and after the first node using the old CTF model, with some deviations between the fit and the power spectrum.
source: In other images, mostly with defocus values under 1 µm and with a sample thickness over 200 nm, CTFFIND4 could fit the power spectrum before and after the first node using the old CTF model, with some deviations between the fit and the power spectrum (Figure 3c).
evidence: This describes CTFFIND4 behavior under specific conditions, shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Fitting the power spectrum with the new model in CTFFIND5 resulted in substantially different estimated CTF parameters and an improved fit for images with defocus under 1 µm and thickness over 200 nm.
source: Fitting the power spectrum with the new model in CTFFIND5 resulted in substantially different estimated CTF parameters and an improved fit, even though the goodness-of-fit estimation did not change.
evidence: This describes the improvement achieved with CTFFIND5 for specific image types.

claim: For some single-particle datasets of large particles, such as the rotavirus double-layered particle, CTFFIND5 can be used to estimate the thickness of the sample, which resulted in CTF fits to higher resolution.
source: We also found that for some single-particle datasets of large particles, such as the rotavirus double-layered particle (Grant and Grigorieff, 2015), we could use CTFFIND5 to estimate the thickness of the sample, which resulted in CTF fits to higher resolution (Figure 3d).
evidence: This describes an application to single-particle data with a citation and reference to Figure 3d.

claim: CTFFIND5 will provide more accurate CTF parameters for images of thick samples, such as those generated from FIB milling.
source: Based on these results we conclude that CTFFIND5 will provide more accurate CTF parameters for images of thick samples, such as those generated from FIB milling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results presented.

claim: The fit in CTFFIND5 provides a direct readout of the specimen thickness, which is important for judging specimen quality and the potential for high-resolution information.
source: In addition, the fit provides a direct readout of the specimen thickness, which is important for judging specimen quality and the potential for high-resolution information that can be recovered from these images.
evidence: This describes a practical benefit of the thickness estimation feature.

claim: The fraction of inelastically scattered electrons can be described by the Beer-Lambert law.
source: The fraction of inelastically scattered electrons can be described by the Beer-Lambert law, which states that the fraction of electrons removed from the image is proportional to the thickness of the sample.
evidence: This is a statement of a physical law used for validation.

claim: The Beer-Lambert law states that the fraction of electrons removed from the image is proportional to the thickness of the sample.
source: The fraction of inelastically scattered electrons can be described by the Beer-Lambert law, which states that the fraction of electrons removed from the image is proportional to the thickness of the sample.
evidence: This is a statement of a physical law.

claim: The apparent mean free path for electron scattering has been experimentally determined for common cryoEM conditions.
source: The apparent mean free path for electron scattering has been experimentally determined for common cryoEM conditions (Rice et al., 2018).
evidence: This references prior experimental work with a citation.

claim: Images that did not follow the linear relationship either contained visible ice contamination, platinum deposits, or they were collected over ice without cellular features and displayed weak Thon rings.
source: Manual inspection of images that did not follow this linear relationship revealed that they either contained visible ice contamination, platinum deposits, or they were collected over ice without cellular features and displayed weak Thon rings.
evidence: This explains outliers in the Beer-Lambert law validation.

claim: The x-axis intercept of the linear model was –14.1 nm, meaning that the node position systematically predicts a smaller thickness than predicted by the Beer-Lambert law.
source: The x-axis intercept of the linear model was –14.1 nm, meaning that the node position systematically predicts a smaller thickness than predicted by the Beer-Lambert law.
evidence: This describes a systematic discrepancy between the two methods.

claim: The mean absolute difference between CTFFIND5 thickness estimates and the linear model was 4.8 nm.
source: To estimate the accuracy of the sample thickness determined by CTFFIND5, we calculated the mean absolute difference to the linear model, which was 4.8 nm.
evidence: This is a quantitative accuracy measurement.

claim: The two approaches (node fitting and Beer-Lambert law) are complementary as they rely on orthogonal mechanisms.
source: Also, the two approaches are complementary as they rely on orthogonal mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the relationship between the two methods.

claim: A linear fit of CTFFIND5 vs tomography thickness revealed a slope of 0.95 and a y-axis intercept of 0.12 nm.
source: A linear fit revealed a slope of 0.95 and a y-axis intercept of 0.12 nm.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the tomography validation.

claim: The CTFFIND5 thickness estimate is on average 1.05× higher than the thickness estimated by tomography.
source: This means that the CTFFIND5 thickness estimate is on average 1.05× higher than the thickness estimated by tomography.
evidence: This is derived from the linear fit results.

claim: Tichelaar et al., 2020, also report that estimating the thickness from the CTF nodes resulted in values roughly 1.1× higher than estimated by tomography.
source: Tichelaar et al., 2020, also report that estimating the thickness from the CTF nodes resulted in values roughly 1.1× higher than estimated by tomography.
evidence: This cites prior work that found a similar systematic difference.

claim: The reasons for the systematic discrepancies between thicknesses estimated by CTFFIND5 and estimates based on the Beer-Lambert law and tomography are unclear.
source: The reasons for the systematic discrepancies between thicknesses estimated by CTFFIND5 and estimates based on the Beer-Lambert law and tomography are unclear, but since they are small and CTFFIND5 estimates lie in between the other two estimates, they will provide comparable information.
evidence: This acknowledges an unexplained systematic difference.

claim: Since the systematic discrepancies are small and CTFFIND5 estimates lie in between the other two estimates, they will provide comparable information.
source: The reasons for the systematic discrepancies between thicknesses estimated by CTFFIND5 and estimates based on the Beer-Lambert law and tomography are unclear, but since they are small and CTFFIND5 estimates lie in between the other two estimates, they will provide comparable information.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the practical utility despite systematic differences.

claim: A simple CTF correction based on CTFFIND defocus estimates obtained from overview images can reduce fringes near biological membranes.
source: We found that a simple CTF correction based on CTFFIND defocus estimates obtained from the overview images can reduce these fringes (Figure 6b).
evidence: This describes an application of CTF correction to overview images, shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Including a Wiener filter-based amplitude correction produces a more naturally looking image that might be best suited to recognize cellular features.
source: However, we found that including a Wiener filter-based amplitude correction described by Tegunov and Cramer, 2019, produces a more naturally looking image that might be best suited to recognize cellular features (Figure 6d).
evidence: This describes a method for improving image appearance with a citation, shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Without estimation of tilt or sample thickness, CTFFIND5 performed CTF estimation roughly within a second.
source: Without estimation of tilt or sample thickness CTFFIND5 performed CTF estimation roughly within a second.
evidence: This is a runtime measurement from benchmarking.

claim: Estimation of the sample thickness adds roughly half a second to the runtime.
source: Estimation of the sample thickness adds roughly half a second to the runtime, therefore allowing CTF estimation within a timeframe comparable to typical exposure times.
evidence: This is a runtime measurement from benchmarking.

claim: Estimation of the tilt increased runtimes substantially to the order of several minutes, due to the exhaustive search of potential tilts over hundreds of power spectra.
source: Estimation of the tilt on the other hand increased runtimes substantially to the order of several minutes, due to the exhaustive search of potential tilts over hundreds of power spectra.
evidence: This is a runtime measurement with an explanation for the increase.

claim: Near real-time tilt estimation can be achieved by using multiple CPU cores.
source: While these runtimes are substantially slower than cryoEM data acquisition, near real-time estimation can be achieved by using multiple CPU cores.
evidence: This suggests a practical solution to the runtime issue.

claim: Optimization of the number of tiles used, better search algorithms, or implementations employing GPUs could increase the speed to the point where real-time estimation is more feasible.
source: Furthermore, optimization of the number of tiles used, better search algorithms, or implementations employing GPUs could increase the speed to the point where real-time estimation is more feasible.
evidence: This speculates about potential future improvements.

claim: The improvements implemented in CTFFIND5 result in more accurate CTF estimation of thick and tilted samples.
source: In summary, the improvements implemented in CTFFIND5 result in more accurate CTF estimation of thick and tilted samples and provide valuable information about the samples to the microscopist.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: CTFFIND5 provides valuable information about the samples to the microscopist.
source: In summary, the improvements implemented in CTFFIND5 result in more accurate CTF estimation of thick and tilted samples and provide valuable information about the samples to the microscopist.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the manuscript.

claim: The new features implemented in CTFFIND5 improve CTF estimation from the power spectra of cryoEM micrographs where assumptions made in CTFFIND4 do not hold.
source: The new features implemented in CTFFIND5 improve CTF estimation from the power spectra of cryoEM micrographs where assumptions made in its predecessor, CTFFIND4, namely a thin and untilted sample, do not hold.
evidence: This is a conclusion statement summarizing the main contribution.

claim: The tilt of the sample is estimated by fitting the CTF to the power spectra calculated from small patches across the image, similar to other software including CTFTilt, Ctfplotter, goCTF, Bsoft, and Warp.
source: The tilt of the sample is estimated by fitting the CTF to the power spectra calculated from small patches across the image, similar to other software including CTFTilt (Mindell and Grigorieff, 2003), Ctfplotter (Mastronarde, 2024; Xiong et al., 2009), goCTF (Su, 2019), Bsoft (Heymann and Belnap, 2007), and Warp (Tegunov and Cramer, 2019).
evidence: This describes the method and compares it to other software with citations.

claim: After estimation of the sample tilt, a tilt-corrected power spectrum is produced that exhibits stronger Thon rings at higher resolution.
source: After estimation of the sample tilt, a tilt-corrected power spectrum is produced that exhibits stronger Thon rings at higher resolution.
evidence: This describes a result of the tilt estimation procedure.

claim: Fitting a modified CTF model that accounts for sample thickness increases the resolution of the fitted regions of the spectra and provides a readout of the sample thickness.
source: To take into account the modulation of the power spectra by thick samples (McMullan et al., 2015; Tichelaar et al., 2020), we fit a modified CTF model, which increases the resolution of the fitted regions of the spectra and provides a readout of the sample thickness.
evidence: This describes the benefit of the thickness estimation feature with citations.

claim: The low exposures (3–5 e-/Å2) typically used in electron cryo-tomography often preclude fitting of sample thickness from power spectra of individual images in the tilt series.
source: While the low exposures (3–5 e-/Å2) typically used in electron cryo-tomography often preclude fitting of sample thickness from power spectra of individual images in the tilt series, we demonstrate that this works reliably for higher exposures (~30 e-/Å2) typically used for 2D template matching (2DTM) (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2017) and in situ single-particle analysis (Cheng et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes a limitation of the method for low-dose imaging with citations.

claim: Thickness fitting works reliably for higher exposures (~30 e-/Å2) typically used for 2D template matching and in situ single-particle analysis.
source: While the low exposures (3–5 e-/Å2) typically used in electron cryo-tomography often preclude fitting of sample thickness from power spectra of individual images in the tilt series, we demonstrate that this works reliably for higher exposures (~30 e-/Å2) typically used for 2D template matching (2DTM) (Lucas et al., 2021; Rickgauer et al., 2017) and in situ single-particle analysis (Cheng et al., 2023).
evidence: This describes where the method works well with citations.

claim: These improvements were mainly developed for 2DTM applied to in situ samples prepared by cryo-FIB milling.
source: We mainly developed these improvements for 2DTM applied to in situ samples, e.g., prepared by cryo-FIB milling.
evidence: This describes the primary motivation for the development.

claim: CTFFIND5 made it possible to quantify sample thickness and tilt parameters for every exposure, which is important information to judge the quality of the lamella before performing time-intensive further processing.
source: Since the sample thickness and sample tilt are apparent from a single exposure, as opposed to a reconstructed tomogram, CTFFIND5 made it possible to quantify these parameters for every exposure. This is important information to judge the quality of the lamella before performing time-intensive further processing (Lucas and Grigorieff, 2023; Tuijtel et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes a practical benefit of the method with citations.

claim: The quality-of-fit estimation of CTFFIND5 goes to higher resolution in tilted and thick samples, making it a better indicator of micrograph quality than the same metric in CTFFIND4.
source: Furthermore, since the quality-of-fit estimation of CTFFIND5 goes to higher resolution in tilted and thick samples (Figures 1c and 3b–d), it is a better indicator of micrograph quality than the same metric in CTFFIND4.
evidence: This describes an improvement in quality assessment with references to figures.

claim: In contrast to software optimized for tilt series data, CTFFIND5 uses no prior information for tilt axis angle and sample tilt, resulting in reduced performance and potentially lower accuracy.
source: In contrast to software optimized for tilt series data, such as Ctfplotter (Mastronarde, 2024), CTFFIND5 uses no prior information for tilt axis angle and sample tilt, resulting in reduced performance and also potential lower accuracy.
evidence: This describes a limitation of CTFFIND5 for tilt series with a citation.

claim: There is no option in CTFFIND5 to pool data from several tilt angles to provide a more accurate defocus or astigmatism estimation.
source: Furthermore, there is no option to pool data from several tilt angles to provide a more accurate defocus or astigmatism estimation.
evidence: This describes another limitation for tilt series applications.

claim: CTFFIND5 together with fit_tilt_model might be useful in troubleshooting angle conventions in tilt series data.
source: However, this also means that CTFFIND5 together with fit_tilt_model might be useful in troubleshooting angle conventions in tilt series data.
evidence: This suggests a potential use case for the software.

claim: Existing pipelines using CTFFIND4 might benefit from the tilt correction in the power spectrum calculation introduced in CTFFIND5, which results in more robust defocus estimation at high tilt.
source: Also, existing pipelines using CTFFIND4 might benefit from the tilt correction in the power spectrum calculation introduced in CTFFIND5, which results in more robust defocus estimation at high tilt (Figure 2).
evidence: This suggests a benefit for existing workflows with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Most single-particle samples are thin and flat and therefore do not benefit from CTFFIND5.
source: While most single-particle samples are thin and flat and therefore do not benefit from CTFFIND5, there might be some samples, such as viral particles (Figure 3d), where direct estimation of the ice thickness is valuable.
evidence: This describes the limited applicability to single-particle samples.

claim: For some single-particle samples, such as viral particles, direct estimation of the ice thickness is valuable.
source: While most single-particle samples are thin and flat and therefore do not benefit from CTFFIND5, there might be some samples, such as viral particles (Figure 3d), where direct estimation of the ice thickness is valuable.
evidence: This describes a potential application to certain single-particle samples with reference to Figure 3d.

claim: Even for thick single-particle samples, the defocus reported by CTFFIND5 is an average for the whole micrograph and per-particle CTF refinement will still be required to recover high-resolution information during averaging.
source: However, even in these cases the defocus reported by CTFFIND5 is an average for the whole micrograph and per-particle CTF refinement, as implemented in cisTEM (Grant et al., 2018), RELION (Zivanov et al., 2018), or CryoSPARC (Punjani et al., 2017; Zivanov et al., 2020), will still be required to actually recover high-resolution information during averaging.
evidence: This describes a limitation and the need for further refinement with citations.

claim: The ability to measure sample tilt might be useful for approaches where a tilted stage is used to overcome preferred particle orientation.
source: The ability to measure sample tilt might be useful for approaches where a tilted stage is used to overcome preferred particle orientation (Tan et al., 2017), as initial per particle defocus values can be derived from the tilt as reported by CTFFIND5 and the particle positions.
evidence: This suggests a potential application with a citation.

source: Power spectra are calculated in 128×128 pixel patches as indicated on a representative micrograph.

source: The tilt-corrected power spectrum exhibits clear peaks at higher spatial resolution than the uncorrected power spectrum, as evident by the 'goodness-of-fit' scores (dashed lines).
